plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 9: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
plan.contextChunk: This figure places three small drawings in a row, each pairing a circle with a straight line rendered as a blue double-headed arrow, to enumerate how many points the two curves can share. In the leftmost drawing the circle is orange and the blue line passes above and to the left of it without ever touching the rim; the label beneath reads "No solutions." In the center drawing the circle is green and the blue line rises steeply from lower left to upper right, grazing the circle at a single point on its upper-left edge, which is marked with a filled black dot; the label beneath reads "One solution." In the rightmost drawing the circle is red and the blue line cuts through it, entering at the lower left and exiting at the upper right; the upper-right crossing is visibly marked with a filled black dot while the second crossing is implied by the line passing through the circle. The label beneath reads "Two solutions." The three panels hold the circle size and the line's slope fixed and change how far the line sits from the center, so the number of circle-line intersections is the variable. Together they lay out the complete range of outcomes for a system built from a circle and a line.

interactionPlan.concept: A line-circle system has zero, one, or two solutions exactly when the perpendicular distance from the circle's center to the line is greater than, equal to, or less than the radius — geometrically the count of intersections, algebraically the sign of the discriminant after substitution.
elements: light x- and y-axes through the origin
circle centered at the origin with fixed radius r, outline color coded by case (red = two solutions, green = one/tangent, orange = none)
blue double-headed straight line of fixed slope whose perpendicular offset from the center is the variable
dashed perpendicular segment from the center to the line, labeled d (distance from center to line)
radius segment or label r on the circle
filled black intersection dot(s) where the line meets the circle (0, 1, or 2 dots)
case caption beneath the figure: 'No solutions' / 'One solution' / 'Two solutions'
equation panel (shown in Equation view): the substituted quadratic in x plus its discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac with sign highlighted
small color legend mapping red/green/orange to two/one/no solutions

interactions.label: Distance d from center to line
interactions.teaches: Dragging the line parallel to itself changes d continuously; the intersection count flips 2 → 1 → 0 precisely as d crosses the radius r, so the distance-to-center versus radius comparison is what controls the number of solutions

interactions.label: Step through cases
interactions.teaches: Visiting the three canonical configurations deliberately shows each as a distinct relationship between line and circle — secant cutting twice, tangent grazing once, external line missing entirely — and marks only the intersection points that actually exist in that case

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching to the equation view reveals that substituting the line into the circle yields a quadratic whose discriminant is positive, zero, or negative in exact correspondence with two, one, or zero intersections — the picture and the algebra count the same solutions

demo_steps.title: Secant: two solutions
demo_steps.narration: With the line passing close to the center (d < r) it cuts the circle at two points, both marked with black dots — the system has two solutions.

demo_steps.title: Tangent: one solution
demo_steps.narration: Step to the tangent case: the line now sits exactly at distance d = r, grazing the rim at a single marked point — exactly one solution.

demo_steps.title: External: no solutions
demo_steps.narration: Step again: the line is pushed out to d > r and no longer touches the circle, so no intersection dots appear — the system has no solution.

demo_steps.title: Sweep it yourself
demo_steps.narration: Drag the distance slider slowly from 0 outward and watch the two dots merge into one at d = r and then vanish — the count changes exactly at the moment the line's distance equals the radius.

demo_steps.title: Same story in algebra
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the equation view: the substituted quadratic's discriminant is positive, zero, or negative in lockstep with two, one, or zero intersections — geometry and algebra are counting the same solutions.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The number of solutions of a line-circle system is just the number of intersections, decided by comparing the line's perpendicular distance from the center to the radius — and that same comparison shows up algebraically as the sign of the discriminant.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single interactive figure (not three static panels): a circle at the origin with a blue double-headed line of fixed positive slope. Color the circle outline by current case — red when two intersections, green when tangent, orange when none — to echo the source's three panels. Draw a thin dashed perpendicular from the center to the line labeled d, and a radius marker labeled r, so the d-versus-r comparison is visible. Place filled black dots only at real intersection points (0, 1, or 2). Caption beneath updates among 'No solutions / One solution / Two solutions'. In Equation view, swap the drawing emphasis for a compact side panel showing the quadratic obtained by substitution and Δ = b² − 4ac with its sign colored (green +, amber 0, red −) to match the geometric case. Keep axes faint so the circle, line, dots, and distance segment dominate.

The figure illustrates possible solution sets for a system of equations involving a circle and a line.

An illustration showing the three possible numbers of intersection points between a line and a circle: zero (no solutions), one (a tangent line), or two (a secant line).

discrepancies: Source is three side-by-side panels (orange 'No solutions', green 'One solution', red 'Two solutions') shown simultaneously; the generated figure collapses these into a single interactive view where only one case is visible at a time behind the slider / case button.
Generated figure adds faint coordinate axes, a dashed perpendicular from center to the line labeled 'd', and a gray radius marker labeled 'r' — none of which appear in the clean source panels.
The in-figure case caption (e.g. 'Two solutions') is small and placed low in the plot, far less prominent than the bold per-panel captions beneath each circle in the source.
Default state shows only the red two-solution case; the orange no-solution and green tangent panels of the source are not visible together at a glance.
evaluation.notes: The line-circle intersection concept, per-case colors (orange/green/red), blue double-headed line, and black solution dots are all faithful and the slider + case button + discriminant view + 5-step player form a rich, correct interactive treatment; the main departures are the single-panel-with-toggle composition versus the source's three simultaneous panels and the added axes/perpendicular/radius chrome, plus small in-figure 'd'/'r'/caption labels.
action_items: Enlarge and bolden the in-figure case caption and place it clearly beneath the circle so it reads like the source's prominent per-panel captions.
Increase the font size and contrast of the 'd' and 'r' annotations so they are comfortably legible at inline size.
Optionally render the three cases as three small side-by-side mini-panels by default (keeping the slider for live exploration) to better match the source's at-a-glance three-panel composition.

feedback.rationale: Overall average of 4.4 with concept_accuracy and interactivity at 5 indicates the figure is strong; the remaining discrepancies (single-panel composition vs three-panel source, added annotation chrome) are minor stylistic choices that don't undermine the interactive treatment's correctness or usability.
